newsitem.title: CANADA: INSTANT VIEW - Canada CPI rises 1.4 pct in August.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Canada CPI rises 1.4 pct in August.

text.p: Following are reactions to a rise in Canada's consumer price index of 1.4 percent in August on a yearly basis, after a rise of 1.2 percent the previous month, as reported by Statistics Canada on Friday.
Economists in a Reuters survey had forecast, on average, a rise of 1.3 percent.

CRAIG WRIGHT, ASSISTANT CHIEF ECONOMIST, ROYAL BANK OF CANADA: "It came in just about where we expected it and shows the domestic economy is still struggling. It suggests the Bank (of Canada) will remain accommodative. Because of that we'll lag any move higher by the Fed (U.S. Federal Reserve).

MICHAEL GREGORY, FIXED INCOME ECONOMIST AND STRATEGIST AT LEHMAN BROTHERS IN TORONTO: "Inflation is not a problem in Canada. Domestic demand is still fragile, therefore I think they (the Bank of Canada) will resist any move to follow the Fed and I think if one had to say where the policy risk is for the Bank it is still probably on a bias to ease. These numbers really don't change that."

PAUL FERLEY, ASSISTANT CHIEF ECONOMIST AT BANK OF MONTREAL: "We have seen a bit of a pick up in the overall measure, but we were getting earlier indications that food and energy prices might rise on a year-over-year basis and that played out. The core (ex-food and energy) showed a bit of a retracement from the jump that we saw last month suggesting that a lot of other prices are still reflecting a lot of slack in the economy. We are still seeing some downward pressure being played out in that core rate resuming its downward trend. So I think that the risks still remain that inflation in Canada could move below the lower band of the Bank of Canada's (one to three percent) target range. The numbers this morning don't suggest the need for any immediate move, but the Bank will still look for opportunities to move on rates when they present themselves."
